analysis.one_liner: Requires taxpayers earning over $1 million a year to pay at least 30% of that income in federal taxes.
analysis.headline: A bill to make millionaires pay at least 30% of their income in federal tax was introduced by 16 Senate Democrats in 2019, sent to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new minimum tax: anyone with adjusted gross income above $1 million would pay at least 30% of that income (after subtracting charitable donations) in combined federal income, minimum, and payroll taxes, phasing in for incomes just above the threshold. It directs the extra revenue toward reducing the deficit, and it also urges Congress to close tax loopholes more broadly. The bill never got any action beyond being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly, because the new revenue would reduce federal deficits that everyone otherwise shares. Taxpayers who comply with the rules also benefit from the bill's stated goal of ensuring high earners cannot use deductions and shelters to pay low effective rates. Charitable giving is protected: taxpayers can subtract their charitable donations before the 30% floor applies, so giving to nonprofits would not be discouraged.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 30% minimum tax on the adjusted gross income of taxpayers earning over $1 million, after allowing charitable deductions, so that very high earners cannot pay low effective rates through deductions and tax preferences.
Phases the tax in gradually for incomes just above $1 million and adjusts the threshold for inflation after 2020, sparing taxpayers close to the line from a sudden jump.
The bill itself states the tax would 'cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year,' revenue that reduces borrowing costs and future burdens shared by all taxpayers.
Includes a nonbinding statement urging Congress to pursue broader tax reform that closes 'unfair and unnecessary tax loopholes' and simplifies the system.

analysis.who_pays: Households and trusts with adjusted gross income above $1 million, who would owe the difference between a 30% minimum on income over the threshold (after charitable deductions) and what they currently pay in income, alternative minimum, and payroll taxes. Because the tax counts all adjusted gross income, this includes owners of pass-through businesses who report business income on their personal returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to adjusted gross income, which includes pass-through business income; a small business owner with a million-dollar gross income but large business expenses or a difficult year could owe the minimum tax despite thinner actual finances, though the phase-in above $1 million softens the first dollars of the hit.

The benefit to ordinary people is indirect: the bill raises no money for programs or tax cuts for working families, and the bill's own estimate of 'billions of dollars a year' in deficit reduction is a claim by its sponsors, not an independent scoring in the record.
The provision expressing the Senate's support for broader loophole-closing tax reform is a nonbinding statement with no legal effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a meaningful tax increase on the roughly one-in-a-hundred taxpayers earning over $1 million, in exchange for deficit reduction that helps everyone a little rather than any family a lot. The design is reasonably careful — a phase-in, an inflation-adjusted threshold, and a charitable-giving carve-out — but the base is adjusted gross income, so owners of pass-through businesses would be swept in even in bad years, and revenue that could fund visible benefits is instead directed at the deficit. It is a modest, well-targeted bill whose cost falls on a small group with the most capacity to pay.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse and 15 Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on June 5, 2019.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action ever appears in the bill's record for the rest of the Congress.
When the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, all unenacted bills expired, and this one was never reintroduced in the record shown.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million a year are better off, because their federal tax burden stayed exactly as it was; they avoided the 30% minimum the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 15 Senate cosponsors; a longtime advocate of a minimum tax on millionaires.

for.name: 15 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors, including Warren, Booker, Klobuchar, Durbin, and Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it the backing of roughly a third of the Senate Democratic caucus.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the entire 116th Congress; the bill's record ends with the referral.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee that received the bill, never scheduled it for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats and no Republican supported the bill on the record; because it never reached a vote, no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: High-income households (over $1 million adjusted gross income)
industries.note: The bill's entire cost falls on this group, which would owe the gap between a 30% minimum on income over $1 million and their current tax bill. Their interest in blocking it runs against the public's interest in the added revenue.

industries.industry: Tax planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: A 30% floor on high earners' taxes would cap the value of deductions, shelters, and planning strategies that this industry sells to very wealthy clients; any tax savings those strategies produced above the floor would be clawed back.

The bill deliberately subtracts charitable contributions before applying the 30% minimum, so donations remain fully deductible for millionaires; the charitable deduction's role for the wealthy is locked in rather than curtailed.
